stimulus.title: Literary Narrative: The Translator
stimulus.text:
For most of my childhood I was my father's voice in English, a job no one assigned me and that I could not have described if anyone had asked. It began, as far as I can reconstruct, at the counter of a pharmacy when I was seven. My father had a prescription in one hand and a dictionary in the other, and the pharmacist, a patient man with a gray mustache, kept repeating a question about allergies more slowly and more loudly, as though volume were a kind of translation. I said the word in our language. My father answered. I said his answer in English. The pharmacist looked at me with an expression I would come to know well: relief mixed with a faint discomfort, as if he had been rescued by someone too small to be holding the rope.

After that, I was summoned to banks, to the landlord's office, to parent-teacher conferences at which I translated my own report card. I became expert in a vocabulary no other child in my class possessed: escrow, deductible, premium, lien. I learned that adults say the most important thing last, after a great deal of preamble, and that if you translate too quickly you miss it. I also learned, though I would not have put it this way, that the person who carries the words between two people holds a small and unofficial power. When the landlord said something cruel, I could soften it. When my father said something proud, I could make it sound polite.

I used that power more often than I like to admit. I told my father the bank teller had been “very sorry” when she had not been sorry at all. I told my teacher my father was “very busy at work” when he was, in fact, too embarrassed to sit in a classroom and be spoken to through his daughter. These were not lies, exactly, or they were the kind of lies that hold a roof up. I was protecting him, I believed, and protecting the strangers, too, from the friction of meeting each other without a cushion.

It took me many years, and in the end a single afternoon, to understand what the cushion had cost. I was nineteen and home from college, and my father needed to dispute a bill from the electric company. I had a summer job and could not come, and so for the first time in my memory he went alone. I spent the afternoon expecting a phone call that never arrived. When I got home he was at the kitchen table, the bill flattened under the sugar bowl, a new figure written beside the old one in his careful hand.

“How did you manage?” I asked, and I could hear in my own voice something I did not like, a note of surprise that was close to condescension. He looked at me for a long moment. “I talked,” he said. “She talked. It was slow. Twice we had to start again.” Then he added, in English, with an accent I had spent years trying to make invisible on his behalf: “She was nice to me. To me, not to you.”

I have thought about that sentence more than almost anything anyone has ever said to me. For years I had imagined that I was building a bridge between my father and the English-speaking world. It had not occurred to me that a bridge can also be a wall, that by standing in the middle of every conversation, I had made sure no one ever spoke to him directly. The clerk at the electric company had not been kinder than the clerks I remembered. She had simply been talking to the person in front of her, and for the first time, that person was him.

I do not regret the years of translating; I am not sure we would have managed without them. But I no longer think of them as purely a gift I gave. They were also something I took, a little at a time, without either of us noticing: the chance for my father to be clumsy, and patient, and understood on his own terms.

I used that power more often than I like to admit. I told my father the bank teller had been “very sorry” when she had not been sorry at all. I told my teacher my father was “very busy at work” when he was, in fact, too embarrassed to sit in a classroom and be spoken to through his daughter. These were not lies, exactly, or they were the kind of lies that hold a roof up. I was protecting him, I believed, and protecting the strangers, too, from the friction of meeting each other without a cushion.

It took me many years, and in the end a single afternoon, to understand what the cushion had cost. I was nineteen and home from college, and my father needed to dispute a bill from the electric company. I had a summer job and could not come, and so for the first time in my memory he went alone. I spent the afternoon expecting a phone call that never arrived. When I got home he was at the kitchen table, the bill flattened under the sugar bowl, a new figure written beside the old one in his careful hand.

“How did you manage?” I asked, and I could hear in my own voice something I did not like, a note of surprise that was close to condescension. He looked at me for a long moment. “I talked,” he said. “She talked. It was slow. Twice we had to start again.” Then he added, in English, with an accent I had spent years trying to make invisible on his behalf: “She was nice to me. To me, not to you.”

I have thought about that sentence more than almost anything anyone has ever said to me. For years I had imagined that I was building a bridge between my father and the English-speaking world. It had not occurred to me that a bridge can also be a wall, that by standing in the middle of every conversation, I had made sure no one ever spoke to him directly. The clerk at the electric company had not been kinder than the clerks I remembered. She had simply been talking to the person in front of her, and for the first time, that person was him.

I do not regret the years of translating; I am not sure we would have managed without them. But I no longer think of them as purely a gift I gave. They were also something I took, a little at a time, without either of us noticing: the chance for my father to be clumsy, and patient, and understood on his own terms.
